title: Jervis Bay turns to fight

facts.text: On 5 November 1940 the German pocket battleship Admiral Scheer found convoy HX 84 in the middle of the North Atlantic.
The convoy had left Halifax, Nova Scotia, on 28 October bound for Britain with 37 or 38 merchant ships, and its only escort was the armed merchant cruiser HMS Jervis Bay.
Jervis Bay was a passenger liner launched in 1922 and armed with old 6 inch guns, while Admiral Scheer carried six 11 inch guns.
Captain Edward Fegen, 49, ordered the convoy to scatter and steered Jervis Bay straight at the raider to draw its fire.
His Victoria Cross citation says: "Crippled, in flames, unable to reply, for nearly an hour the Jervis Bay held the German's fire."
Jervis Bay was sunk and 190 of her men died, Fegen among them.
During the night the neutral Swedish freighter Stureholm, under Captain Sven Olander, turned back to search and picked up 65 survivors, landing them at Halifax on 12 November.
Most of the convoy escaped in the dusk; Admiral Scheer sank five of its ships: Beaverford, Fresno City, Kenbane Head, Maidan and Trewellard.
The tanker San Demetrio, loaded with aviation fuel, was set ablaze and abandoned, but two days later 16 of her crew in one lifeboat found her still burning, climbed back aboard and put out the fire.
With no charts or navigation instruments, they steered San Demetrio home and brought her into the Clyde on 16 November; their story became the 1943 film San Demetrio London.
Fegen was awarded the Victoria Cross after his death, announced on 22 November 1940, "for valour in challenging hopeless odds and giving his life to save the many ships it was his duty to protect."
Admiral Scheer went on raiding Allied shipping for months and did not return to Germany until spring 1941.
